segments: Recovering from a failed system update: reverting flake.lock is a common way to restore a reproducible state, but it does not mean the system itself has been rolled back.
What flake.lock Really Is
flake.lock is plain-text JSON for nix to read: nix cares about its contents, not where it came from. You can:
Edit it manually (change rev, URL, or narHash)
Revert it with git checkout (the preferred option)
Copy a lock file from elsewhere
As long as narHash matches rev and the packages can be built, nix will use it.
Rollback Method One: git checkout (Preserve Current Changes First)
If your configuration is in a git repository, prefer restoring flake.lock from a known-good Git revision:
Why this is the safest approach:
The specified commit is a known-working version from before the update
No need to guess narHash
Git history provides traceability
Rollback Method Two: Roll Back the System Generation
If the problem is in the system itself, rather than just dependency locking, you can roll back the entire generation:
For the full tutorial, see the Generation Management Guide. If the new system will not boot at all, reboot and select an older generation in the GRUB menu ("NixOS - All configurations").
Garbage Collection Warning

NixOS generations are "stacked": each switch creates a new generation, and older ones are retained until explicitly deleted. GC reclaims only store paths that are no longer referenced by roots. Do not run nix-collect-garbage before an important configuration update. Ordinary GC does not delete paths still referenced by generations; nix-collect-garbage -d deletes old generations and reclaims unreferenced content, potentially removing your rollback path.
Pitfalls of Manual Editing

narHash must be correct: nix uses narHash to verify downloaded content. If rev changes but narHash is still the old value, you get a hash mismatch. Manually changing rev usually requires a corresponding new narHash.
Dedicated Commands Mean Manual Editing Is Not Always Necessary
Roll back to a specific commit: 在 flake.nix 中将 nixpkgs.url 固定到 github:NixOS/nixpkgs/<rev>，再运行 nix flake update nixpkgs
However, declaring inputs and letting Nix generate the lock file is usually easier to review than editing JSON manually, since the configuration itself is in a git repository.
flake.lock is a version lockfile: it locks each input to an exact version for reproducibility. Editing it manually means manually changing the locked version, which is entirely valid.
Operation Reference
Operation
Method
Revert to an older, known-good version
git restore --source=<commit> -- flake.lock (overwrites this file in the working tree; back it up first)
Update to the latest version
Update a single input
Manually change a specific rev
Edit manually, with the corresponding narHash (cumbersome; use sparingly)

The key point: if your configuration is in a git repository, prefer restoring flake.lock from a known-good Git revision rather than editing it manually. Manual editing is more of an "advanced technique" and is usually unnecessary.
